title: County Weighs ICE Program: Officials Seek Details on 287(g) Jail Enforcement Model Before Considering Public Comment and Vote
author: Andrea Grabenstein
content:
County weighs ICE Program: Officials seek details on 287(g) jail enforcement model before considering public comment and vote

 September 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 654
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Queen Anne's County officials say they are seeking more information from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement about the county's eligibility for a 287(g) Jail Enforcement Model program.At an informal community forum Sept. 29 hosted by Eastern Shore Indivisible at the Kent Island branch of the Queen Anne's County Public Library, County Commissioner President Chris Corchiarino and Sheriff Gary Hofmann updated residents on the status of discussions with ICE.
Corchiarino said the county has not yet been told whether it qualifies for the Jail Enforcement Model, one of three agreements available under ICE's 287(g) program. He emphasized that no plans are in place.
"We're waiting to hear from federal officials," Corchiarino said. "We don't have clear details or expectations yet of what a memorandum of understanding would look like."
Program background
Under the Jail Enforcement Model, correctional officers can be deputized with limited federal authority to serve civil detainers within a county detention facility. Other models under 287(g) include the Warrant Service Officer and Task Force programs, though Corchiarino said Queen Anne's is not pursuing those.
On July 30, the county's Republican Central Committee hosted an informational meeting in Stevensville with James Brooks, community relations officer for ICE's Washington and Baltimore field offices. Following that session, Corchiarino said, residents asked county leaders to seek more information about the county's eligibility.
He noted that requirements for correctional facilities vary by jurisdiction in Maryland. In Queen Anne's County, the detention center falls under the authority of the county commissioners rather than law enforcement.
"If we find out we're not eligible, then it's a moot point," Corchiarino said. "If we are eligible, then we'll need to look at requirements and a cost analysis. Any decision would go through public comment and ultimately a commission vote."
There is no set timeline, he said, adding that even if ICE responds soon, the matter would take time before reaching an agenda.
Community questions and concerns
During the forum, some residents voiced concerns about immigration enforcement and civil rights. One man who identified himself as part of the Hispanic community said he had been detained twice "on the west side of the bridge" and carried laminated copies of his birth certificate out of fear.
"What's going to be done to ensure I keep my American rights … without being afraid of the lights in the rearview mirror?" he asked, drawing applause.
Hofmann said the sheriff's office does not have authority to serve civil detainers and in his 30 years could recall only one case involving an ICE civil detainer in the county. He stressed that the role of ICE is separate from the role of county commissioners or the sheriff's office.
"Regardless of origin, whether American or immigrant, there are bad people with warrants for crimes, and we are obligated to enforce the criminal law," Hofmann said.
He added that ICE falls under the umbrella of Homeland Security Investigations and that since 2010 the county sheriff's office has had a designated desk for Homeland Security agents, used in rare but valuable partnerships on cases involving fraud, child pornography and human trafficking.
"What I don't want to do is create fear amongst our community," Hofmann said. "We want people to get the services they need here in Queen Anne's County. We are genuinely here to take care of everyone fairly and equally."
Calls for transparency
Some residents said they want more public collaboration when federal topics arise.
"This affects everyone. It's not just Republicans or Democrats. We should be working together to protect our community," one Grasonville woman said.
A Centreville woman added that she wanted reassurance county law enforcement would remain lawful and not adopt questionable tactics she had heard about elsewhere.
Corchiarino said he considers public input an important factor in any decision.
"A room full of people, that's persuasive for me," he said.
Silvia Gonzalez Roman, co-founder of Eastern Shore Indivisible, said the group invited an ICE representative to the forum but did not receive a response.
"Building community with open dialogue is what it is all about," she said.

title: MACo Leaders Meet with Talbot Officials to Discuss 2026 General Assembly
author: Konner Metz
content:
MACo leaders meet with Talbot officials to discuss 2026 General Assembly

 September 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 536
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Leaders from the Maryland Association of Counties shared predictions for a calmer legislative session in 2026 during a meeting with the Talbot County Council on Tuesday.Michael Sanderson, MACo's executive director, and Jack Wilson, the association's president and current Queen Anne's County commissioner, met for an annual check-in with Talbot officials.
Sanderson reminded the council members of last year's volatile General Assembly session, during which legislators and Gov. Wes Moore (D) had to reckon with closing a $3 billion gap in the state's fiscal year 2026 budget.
Some savings came through cost shifts placing more burden on county governments, the MACo leaders said. But they added that the upcoming 2026 session, and the fiscal year 2027 budget that goes along with it, likely won't be as dire.
"Relatively calm, probably not a big crisis," Sanderson said of his projection for this year's session, which officially kicks off Jan. 14 in Annapolis.
He said the large budgetary concerns are likely to reappear in 2027 as legislators put together a plan for fiscal year 2028.
"The story from last year is gonna repeat itself, but with a year off," Sanderson predicted.
Specifically, the executive director said Maryland's expansive education funding formula, The Blueprint, will influence the 2027 session. And in the short-term, some counties are already coming to grips with increasing cost shares for education.
"Every county is either in the midst or a year or two away from seeing a year where the increase in school spending required under Blueprint requires all the money or even more money than your county's likely to gain in revenue for that year," Sanderson said. "It's an obvious squeeze at the local level."
Talbot County's fiscal year 2026 budget included $55 million in education funding required by The Blueprint's formulas. On top of that, the council approved an additional $600,000 in funding to fill new positions.
That mark had been scaled back twice from the original ask the Talbot Board of Education made of the council — first requesting $5.5 million in supplementary funds, then $1.1 million.
County Council Vice President Pete Lesher, who supported the district's $1.1 million request earlier this year, said it was "short-sighted" for the county to only fund the district's request partially, given that Blueprint requirements are only set to increase in future years. But other council members opted to hold back on dedicating the full request as the county aimed to even out its spending hikes seen in years prior.
Sanderson said on Tuesday that housing legislation will be at the forefront this winter. Recently, Moore signed an executive order that aims to speed up the permitting and building of affordable housing projects.
"I anticipate that being a big fight," Sanderson said. "Whether it's a big fight in the more rural jurisdictions is yet to be seen."
Council Member Lynn Mielke asked how Easton fits into state plans to tackle the housing issue.
Sanderson said there's an opportunity for MACo to advocate for provisions so a potential housing package doesn't "overwhelm" local jurisdictions. He said the association can help push for certain changes to help counties and towns that lack authority in certain areas, such as the variation of impact fees on developers.
"At the same time, we generally want to keep land use decisions local," he added.

title: Historical Society Relationship and Regional Detention Center Update
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Historical Society relationship and Regional Detention Center update

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 389

 Read News Document

 Denton — The Caroline County Historical Society wants to rebuild a working relationship with the County Commissioners so they can get some help funding for different projects to help bring tourist to the town."We have in and around Preston a five-mile radius the most significant components of the Underground Railroad in the United States," lifetime member of the historical society Mick McCrea said.
The Linchester Mill historical sight offers many trails and buildings to where Harriet Tubman and other prominent individuals lived.
"We have actual buildings you can literally walk in the footsteps of people where they stayed in the homes where they got freedom from," McCrea said.
Another suggestion made by historical society board member David "Gene" Harris that the Linchester Mill pond be restored for many reasons.
"If we ever had a major fire, the Linchester Mill pond would be an ideal spot to recharge their fire trucks," Harris said.
The County Commissioners want to establish a working relationship as well, a big component is funding and both sides will plan to work together in the future to help with the Linchester historical sight.
Potential Regional Detention Center updateThe potential Regional Detention Center came up in discussion again for the commissioners.
The center would be located at the former Eastern Pre-Release Unit site at 700 Flat Iron Square Road near Church Hill and would house detainees from Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent counties. It aims to address the growing need for modern and efficient detention facilities in the region, where counties are struggling to finance renovations or replacements of their aging detention facilities.
The commissioners said they still have not received exact numbers for how much everything will cost and how much the county will save by joining the agreement with the other counties.
Caroline County Commission Vice President Larry Porter suggested that the county should do an independent evaluation of the operating cost.
"This decision is going to depend on the operational cost and I'm talking long range operational cost," Porter said. "Would it make sense for us to engage someone to do an independent evaluation of these operating cost?"
The county also want numbers crunched on transportation, employment and other things.
"The biggest question we all have is the operating side of the detention center," Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox said.
The county will have Fox run an independent evaluation to get some calculated numbers to the administrators.

title: QAC Regulates Short Term Rentals, Establishes Animal Abuse Registry
author: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
QAC regulates short term rentals, establishes animal abuse registry

 December 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 316
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Centreville — Detailing onsite parking requirements, guest occupancy, annual inspections and amplified music curfew, Queen Anne's County Commissioners approved an ordinance regulating short term rentals in the county Nov. 26.Making short term rentals permitted in all county zoning districts and dwelling units, the intent of the ordinance is to address short-term rentals in the county with a focus on protecting existing neighborhoods and addressing enforcement.
In an effort to avoid potential Chesapeake Bay Bridge traffic snarls, an approved amendment requires the property owner or a property manager be located in Queen Anne's County and available at all times during occupancy.
Commissioner Jack Wilson clarified property managers can be as simple as a neighbor within the county available to respond to the property. "It doesn't have to be someone professional that you're paying to do it," he said.
Short term rental property owners must receive a zoning certificate annually and additional special events approval is separate conditional use.
Short term rentals must register with the finance office who will collect the hotel tax.
The ordinance includes public comment correspondence from Nov. 12.
While county ordinances typically go into effect within 46 days, understanding time constraints, all short term rental owners will be notified of ordinance requirements including inspection scheduling for a flexible roll out period over the next few months, according to County Administrator Todd Mohn.
In other business, working toward the safety of animals, the commissioners also approved an ordinance establishing a county animal abuse registry.
The ordinance noted factual data that supports being found guilty of abusing animals can also potentially reflect cruelty to humans, in addition to being likely to abuse animals again in the future.
Similar to child abuse registry, the animal abuse registry will provide accountability to those found guilty of animal abuse in the past, Commissioner Phil Dumenil said, and considered the registry a "huge step in the right direction" in protecting animals from getting in the wrong hands.

title: Local legislators reflect on General Assembly
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Local legislators reflect on General Assembly

 April 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 629
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — On Wednesday morning, the Caroline County Chamber of Commerce hosted a Legislative Wrap-up Breakfast with Maryland senators and delegates from the Eastern Shore.The meeting provided a summary and discussion of the recent Maryland state legislative session, the General Assembly. Topics discussed included DAF residual legislation and solar energy.
Sens. Stephen Hershey (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline) and Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), along with Dels. Jay Jacobs (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), Steven Arentz (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), Christopher T. Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Jefferson Ghrist (R-36, Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), were in attendance.
Jacobs spoke on his work on the Environmental and Transportation Committee and the work both delegates and local leadership in Caroline County had on regulating dissolved air flotation, or DAF, residuals.
"I really do appreciate the fact that all three county commissioners and Caroline County were there because it had a huge impact on the committee in Annapolis," Jacobs said. "With an issue that meant that much to the county, all three county commissioners showed up and gave very compelling testimony as to the real problem."
DAF is a method for processing wastewater from food processing plants. The method leaves behind a sludge-like byproduct, or DAF residuals.
House Bill 991 and its pair, Senate Bill 1074, aim to establish a food processing residuals utilization permit authorizing the Department of Agriculture to issue the permits, develop a fee schedule and inspect any site where food processing residuals are utilized.
This bill is significant to the residents of Caroline County, who have raised concerns about the storage of dissolved air flotation residuals and other waste materials.
The Caroline County Commissioners introduced legislation on Feb. 6 to establish four moratoriums related to DAF residuals, vegetable processing wastewater and the storage of biosolids not permitted by the Department of the Environment.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter said he met with Del. Sara Love (D-Montgomery); Alan Girard, Eastern Shore director at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation; and a Caroline County Department of Planning and Codes representative to discuss the draft legislation.
The bill is awaiting final approval by Governor Wes Moore to sign into law.
SOLAR DEVELOPMENT
Delegates expressed concerns over legislation they said took away a vital part of the comprehensive solar development planning process, giving local communities less determination over solar expansion.
Jacobs spoke on Senate Bill 783, or the Brighter Tomorrow Act, which would lower the cost of developing Maryland solar projects and increase the value of solar energy for consumers across the state.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter, who was in attendance, argued that if counties are forced to have more solar, they should be able to negotiate and charge what they want from solar facilities. SB 783 attempted to limit taxes charged to commercial solar facilities.
"I made a comment in the committee: If solar was as good as we are told it's good … Why doesn't everybody in this room have it?" Arentz said. "We're pushing so hard for something we can do. And I think the General Assembly has to, at some point, wake up."
The state's Renewable Portfolio Standard had already established a nation-leading mandate to deploy solar that equals 14.5% of Maryland's electric demand by 2030. Maryland has fallen behind the pace to meet that goal, only meeting 55% of the policy's intermediate 2022 target.
After the delegates had reflected on this year's legislative session, Arentz expressed his appreciation to his fellow delegates for the work that was accomplished during the legislative session.
"I appreciate the time. You guys are wonderful. And as these guys said, this is kind of a love fest. We do it here. We do it up in Cecil County. And we're very, very lucky because we have a lot of like-minded people to communicate, we talk, and we work well together," he said.

title: Shelter Seeing Success
author: Andrea Grabenstein
content:
Shelter seeing success

 March 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein | Section: News 
 
 705
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Centreville — Queen Anne's County animals continue to be in "good paws" as officials presented updates to ensure the safety and wellbeing of those in their care to the Queen Anne's Board of County Commissioners Feb 27.The Queen Anne's County Animal Control Commission (ACC) introduced updates to the Animal Control Comprehensive plan, Chapter 9.
While there have certainly been changes over the years, the Animal Control ordinance has never seen a line by line holistic review of documents such as this before, said Jennifer Nowak, commission chair.
"It needed a major upgrade," she said.
Revisions were especially needed to make the ordinance more applicable for animal control cases, Nowak noted. The extensive revision includes housekeeping items and definition changes to make the documentation flow better.
Updates to the animal control ordinance include three full document reviews, hundreds of hours of work and strong collaboration from officials including Animal Control, emergency services and animal services, according to Nowak.
A public hearing regarding the ordinance is expected at the commissioner's March 26 meeting.
In other business, Queen Anne's County Animal Services (QACAS) presented 2023 overviews and 2024 projections to the county commissioners.
Animal Services Chief of Services Kelly Hamilton presented a year in review and projections for the shelter moving forward.
The shelter continues to lead the way in providing care care for forlorn animals of the Eastern Shore with an impact stronger than ever, she said, it was a very successful year of diligent volunteers, engaging events, and successful community support and 2024 only looks to continue.
The organization considers itself a quintessential No-Kill Shelter of the state of Maryland and the Eastern Shore, Hamilton said, with the Live Release Rate determined by the number of animals leaving the shelter via adoption, returned to the owner or transferred to another shelter.
The national standard to be considered a No Kill Shelter is 90% and with a 94.6% rate, QACAS is proud to be one of 12 such shelters in Maryland, she said.
A total of 1,324 animals entered the county's shelter in 2023, whether as strays, seized or transferred in, a 29% increase from 2022, according to Hamilton.
Through QACAS, 679 animals found their "furr-ever" families in 2023, she announced.
Nearly 900 surgeries were performed onsite ranging from routine neuters, to life saving procedures.
The shelter has ramped up its social media presence including facial recognition software to instrumentally connect owners and pets and help 166 animals find their way back home in 2023.
"It's amazing, the technology is there," Hamilton said.
Hamilton credited volunteers and foster families as the "true heroes" for their tireless dedication to the animals.
"It really takes our team to invest all this time and energy in these animals to get them ready for that adoption floor," she said.
Foster families are imperative to provide valuable insight into an animal's behavior outside of the shelter to provide "purr-fect" placement for prospective adopters.
Programs include doggy day trips in hopes of enticing new foster families with a day of play away from the kennels, which can often snowball into full blown adoptions.
IQACAS participated in a National Clear the Shelter Event to roaring success, seeing nearly 100 animals find homes in a very short amount of time, she said.
Other community events include Puppy Yoga, donation drives, and partnering with the Parks and Recreation Department for the first annual "Pawing in Love" Fun Run.
Moving forward, the shelter expects to see an increase in community involvement including school education programs and "bigger and better" fundraisers, Hamilton said.
The facility has undergone remodeling to include updated in house dental machines and a new lobby layout. The shelter is now home to new cat condos, improved yard spaces, and even surround sound speakers at the dog kennels to provide calming ambiance.
With its newly improved yard space, they plan to offer additional enrichment programs for dog training including daily doggie play groups.
A complimentary behaviorist class is available for all newly adopted dogs. This program will serve residents who may be considering surrendering animals to the shelter for behavioral concerns or are in need of training tips, according to Hamilton.
QACAS looks to continue leading the pack as a local No Kill Shelter with updated technology and infrastructure improvements to provide community critters the best care "pawsible."
More information about the QACAS, including upcoming events can be found at www.qac.org/1425/Animal-Services.

title: Comptroller Highlights Changes During Tour of Queen Anne's County
author: DOUG BISHOP dbishop@chespub.com
content:
Comptroller highlights changes during tour of Queen Anne's County

 January 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DOUG BISHOP dbishop@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 607
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Maryland Comptroller Brooke Lierman visited four establishments in Queen Anne's County on Dec. 20: the newly opened YMCA in Centreville, Everside Health Center also in Centreville, and two local businesses on Kent Island, both located in the Chesapeake Bay Business Park — Italberco, a growing sweet-tooth business working with the food industry providing dessert ingredients and Queen Anne's County's largest employer, Paul Reed Smith Guitars.Her visit began at the YMCA, where she met with YMCA Mid-Shore Region Executive Director Robbie Gill; two Queen Anne's County commissioners, Chris Corchiarino and Jack Wilson; Queen Anne's County Administrator Todd Mohn; county Economic Development and Tourism Director Heather Tinelli; and Queen Anne's Community Services Director Cathy Willis. The meeting was "a working lunch" served at the Y.
During the lunch, Lierman spoke about the changes made within the comptroller's office in the past year. Several new positions have been created, including a chief information officer. She said that the Comptroller's Office is striving for "more transparency."
Beginning in February, for the first time ever, businesses will be able to pay their taxes online.
"We are also preparing, in the Comptroller's Office, a designed plan for future prosperity for the state," Lierman said, "not a plan for just the next four years, but far beyond that."
Lierman has been visiting each of Maryland's 23 counties over the past year, sharing a similar message.
She expressed concern in an interview with the Bay Times and Record Observer that the state deficit is mounting, beginning with the 2024 state budget. Former Maryland Gov. Larry Hogan left the state with a surplus. However, that surplus has since disappeared.
Before the Hogan administration left office, the General Assembly passed massive legislation for new state funding for public schools, which will kick-in in 2024.
She said, "The governor and I will need to speak about what we're going to do. It will be either to cut state services, or find new sources of revenue."
She didn't mention anything about raising taxes when mentioning "new sources of revenue."
Wilson spoke about efforts in Queen Anne's County to help restore the Chesapeake Bay and suggested Lierman come back to go out with some watermen to witness oyster seeding that is helping cleanse the bay waters. He also spoke about concerns with local farmers on the issue of solar panels being erected near preservation farmlands within the county.
Wilson praised the newly established Everside Health program, which is now covering all county government and public school employees. Queen Anne's is the first county in Maryland to become part of the Everside Health benefits. It was mentioned that Everside is about to cover six other Maryland counties.
Wilson spoke about the Queen Anne's Chamber of Commerce looking into Everside covering local small businesses within the county to help with health care benefits for their employees.
Corchiarino spoke briefly about the issues concerning the Chesapeake Bay Bridge. He said, "The effects of bridge traffic are crippling to Queen Anne's County."
Lierman said, "As of Jan. 3, there will be a published 'State of the Economy' report presented to the public, providing residents with both good and bad outlooks for the state going forward."
She mentioned that there are 12 comptroller offices within the state. The Eastern Shore office is located in Salisbury. The closest office to Queen Anne's County is in Annapolis.
Lierman was elected the state's first female comptroller in November 2022. She was a state delegate previously for eight years, representing part of Baltimore City. She is the mother of two children, a boy, 11, and girl, 6. Lierman grew-up in Montgomery County.
After the meeting at the Y, Lierman visited and toured the other three facilities, gathering information about their business successes.

title: Residents Protest Planned Royal Farms Development, Citing Safety Concerns
author: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Residents protest planned Royal Farms development, citing safety concerns

 April 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 328
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Bay Bridge Cove residents took to the streets in Stevensville to protest a potential Royal Farms development before a Queen Anne's County Planning and Zoning technical meeting April 16.On April 14 and 15 preceding the meeting, about a dozen residents each day from the 55-and-older community demonstrated outside their neighborhood to oppose the project, said coordinator Teresa Tamburrino.
Traffic in the area is "already contentious," she said.
A county Staff Technical Advisory Committee meeting brought together local and state agencies to discuss technical aspects of the development proposal, including representatives from the Departments of Public Works and Parks and Recreation and the State Highway Administration.
The applicant is proposing to combine three parcels at 336 Romancoke Road (Route 8) in Stevensville for a 5,154-square-foot convenience store, six gasoline fuel islands with 12 fueling positions, and a 1,248-square-foot car wash located at the rear of the convenience store.
The Queen Anne's County Planning Commission previously tabled a decision on the concept plan for another Royal Farms convenience store on Kent Island in December 2022.
The county received extensive public input regarding the project, according to Planning Director Amy Moredock. The room was packed with concerned citizens and surrounding business owners Wednesday.
Major concerns the board continued to address with the developers included traffic impact on Maryland Route 8, entrance and exit access, and architectural issues.
The proposal is not before the County Commissioners for a vote, and due to subsequent comments from the planning commission that must be addressed, the Royal Farms project is not expected to be placed on an agenda for some time, Moredock said.
Bay Bridge Cove residents and members of the Homeowners Association there plan to seek information about a potential county ordinance to prevent gas stations within 500 feet of a day care center, Tamburrino said.
Residents are also compiling data and crash statistics to prepare for the next meeting, according to Tamburrino.
More information and updates can be found on the Planning and Zoning Department section of the county website at qac.org.

Centreville Planning Commission tables cannabis expansion

 January 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 660
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Centreville cannabis dispensary Green Thumb Industries request for major site plan approval for a two-acre expansion was tabled Jan. 15 by the Centreville Planning Commission to address additional comments.The original facility final site plan was approved in 2021 with two-acres of outdoor growth, and Green Thumb is now requesting amended final minor site plan to expand with an additional two acres and include a new irrigation shed and incorporate drying trailers to enclose order, according to attorney Kevin Shearon, DMS Associates on behalf of the applicant.
The expansion is a permitted use and meets town requirements, he said.
Public comment was split on the expansion.
Several emails from citizens presented to the planning commission voiced support, citing Green Thumb as a job creator and revenue source for the town, as well as cannabis fitting into the expanding definition of agriculture.
In-person public comment largely played a different tune however, mainly residents of Symphony Village speaking against the odor.
Over the summer odors were described as minimal or not as noticeable, but during September to December of the harvest and drying time, residents claimed the order as "pungent" and "almost daily."
In operation in Centreville for a year and a half, Green Thumb has undergone major odor mitigations following previous community feedback, spending over $100,000 assessing, identifying and installing technology, according to Rebecca Brown, of Green Thumb's government affairs department.
Green Thumb has invested over $40 million in the building, she said.
The location had been vacant for eight years before Green Thumb moved in, Brown said. The location was chosen for the Green Thumb's ability to grow as expansion is a key component of the business model and needed to stay competitive, she said.
Green Thumb is considered one of the largest private employers in town and in the county, employing over 200 at the Comet Drive location, Brown said.
Byers Scientific performs the testing samples both indoor and outdoor for Green Thumb twice a year previously in June, Brown said.
While odor hasn't completely gone away, Green Thumb was doing everything it could to diminish odors, "and we're not going to stop doing that," according to Brown.
Smells have been identified as coming from harvesting and processing, not just budding outside, Green Thumb officials said, and mitigation has been applied where odors have been noted to be the most prevalent including the extraction lab, and the indoor kitchen hood, where edible products are created.
Green Thumb previously utilized a cost-prohibited hemp dryer, while moving forward, seeks to use fully enclosed drying containers with charcoal odor mitigation built in, according to officials.
Scrubbing the air, the 40-foot long, eight-foot wide containers perform roughly 42 air changes per hour and filters are swapped out every two weeks, officials said.
The same odor mitigation technology already employed will be utilized on a broader scale, she said.
Brown claimed with the expansion, twice that outdoor growing area would not double the odor, "It's sort of like when you bake two apple pies versus you bake four apple pies, you're not going to smell any additional pies, you're already smelling it."
Acknowledging she was not in the marijuana industry, planning commission member Wendy Emerson disagreed with the pie analogy, stating herself as a baker, and that "four pies will in fact provide more scent."
Emerson sought information regarding the industry's standards that she claimed should have been shared with the planning commission prior, including what was the odor level previously, where is it today, and what is the intended increase.
Noting existing technology to detect other odors such as carbon monoxide monitors, Emerson sought exploring technology to monitor cannabis odors and Brown said Green Thumb could look into technology as part of the expansion's approval.
The planning commission also noted the plan's public works agreement and tree canopy requirements need addressing.
Tabling a vote, the planning commission determined there was not enough information and sought additional comments to be addressed including testing data from other Green Thumb sites during the fall months and submission of the most recent Jan. 20 test results.

 Centreville — On Dec. 12, major site plan approval was granted by the Queen Anne's County Planning Commission to Chesapeake Bay Beach Club LLC for its proposal to construct a four-story, 32-room hotel with a bathhouse on Marina Club Road in Stevensville.Located on Kent Island south of Route 50, southeast of the Chesapeake Bay Bridge, the proposed hotel project will cover 2.1 acres on Marina Club Road in Stevensville, according to Rob Gunter, principal development review planner.
The project was last presented to the Planning Commission in April for concept plan approval in which allocation for the project's public water and sewer was also granted.
Along the south side of the proposed 25,727-square-foot hotel will be an attached 868 square foot bathhouse.
The rear of the hotel will include an outdoor area of a pool, terrace, lawn areas, outdoor seating, fire pit and outdoor fireplace.
Located in the Airport Protection and the Kent Island Gateway Zoning District within the Chester-Stevensville Growth Area, the entire area is located within the Chesapeake Bay Critical Area and is designated as an intensely developed area, as well as a modified buffer area.
The site is within the Chester-Stevensville Growth Area and is located in a priority funding area and Queen Anne's County's designated enterprise zone.
An existing office building will be removed and parking reconfigured to accommodate the site plan, Gunter said.
The project provides an excess of 31 parking spaces on-site and is proposing to enter into a shared parking agreement with the Chesapeake Bay Bridge Marina.
Developer Dereck Janes noted it was already not uncommon to have near zero parking availability on site on weekends.
The appearance of a full parking lot can have an effect on business, with potential customers taking their business elsewhere, Janes said.
All dimensional and zoning district standards have been met, Gunter said, and the Planning Commission granted major site plan approval, with findings including the proposed use would not increase traffic hazards and was consistent with the Comprehensive Plan.
The hotel's name Wilson's Cove is in honor of the late John Wilson, the original developer of the Chesapeake Bay Beach Club, according to Kevin Shearon of DMS and Associates.

Grasonville proposal looks to develop farmland for infill affordable housing

 December 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Local News

 GRASONVILLE — A proposed water and sewer amendment to supply a potential affordable housing development in Grasonville gained support during a public hearing Dec. 10.The proposal is to amend the property's water and sewer services to accommodate the development of 72 townhomes and 218 single family lots.
Located at 5400 Main Street, Aspire at Ewing Farm is a 112 acre property currently used for agriculture and is zoned Grasonville Planned Residential Neighborhood.
Flows from use are anticipated to be 72,500 gallons per day. Sewer service would be provided via a constructed gravity sewer pump station and water service would he provided by the Grasonville water system.
Sketch plan approval for the project was granted by the Queen Anne's County Planning Commission in October and met requirements of the Water and Sewer Master Plan.
The property has been part of the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan for a 10 year service since 2011, according to attorney Joe Stevens on behalf of developer K. Hovnanian.
The property has been ratified as part of the Grasonville Growth Area and zoned for planned residential development for decades.
The 2022 Comprehensive Plan highlights affordable housing as a high need in the county.
According to Mike Irons, division president of K. Hovnanian Homes of Maryland, LLC the Aspire Development will include "efficient homes without a lot of bells and whistles," aimed toward first time home buyers, workforce housing and affordable housing.
"We're bringing to the market something that the county needs," Irons said.
K. Hovnanian is also the builder and developer for the 55 and older Four Seasons Community.
Barry Griffith, planner with Lane Engineering, noted the location is an infill property surrounded by existing houses, schools and parks.
"We're a hole in a donut of development around us, and that's where we want new growth to go," Griffith said.
The property is located in a priority funding area, meaning the state and county have both acknowledged it as appropriate for state funding for future growth, he said.
Member of the Ewing family Mitchell Andrew noted the Ewings have been approached by local, regional and national developers over the years and "without a doubt" K. Hovnanian was the first that "really fit Grasonville," and met the needs of the county.
The public hearing saw over 10 in-person as well as six emails from residents voicing support for the amendment to move the development forward with resounding sentiment toward the county's need for affordable housing.
Agreeing the project met the needs of the county, Commission President Jim Moran noted the loose terminology of affordable housing that could change in the potentially two years before the development is ready.
Following potential commissioner amendment approval for sewer and water redesignation, the project would then move forward for additional approvals including site plan, subdivision and, Adequate Public Facilities Ordinance.
A public hearing was also held to consider amending the Queen Anne's County 2011 Comprehensive Water and Sewer Plan for Barnstable Lowery Farm's proposed development of 82 townhomes on a 11 acre lot in Main Street Chester.
The property is agricultural land consisting of two farms on either side of the three improved properties that are not included in the development proposal. The proposed development is part of Lowery Farm and Dream Farm. The portion adjacent to Main Street is zoned Town Center and the parcel to the rear of the site is zoned Countryside.
All residential development will occur in the Town Center zoning district.
Sewer services would be provided by Vacuum Sewer Collection Station 'G' and water services would be provided by the Stevensville/Chester water system.
Flows from the use are anticipated at 20,500 gallons per day.
The Planning Commission granted concept plan approval for the Barnstable Townhouse development in October and no anticipated off-site sewer or water infrastructure issues are associated with this proposal.
At public comment, Tracy Schulz, on behalf of Dream Farm ownership, spoke in favor of the project, citing the development appropriate for the area.
One email voiced concern for future developments' impact on water and sewer services on Kent Island, Grasonville, and Queenstown, and recommended posting projected usage numbers.
Public comment is still being accepted and a commissioner vote is expected at the Jan. 14 meeting.

title: Public Hearing Discusses Short Term Rental Regulations
author: Andrea Grabenstein
content:
Public hearing discusses short term rental regulations

 November 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 499
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Following favorable recommendation by the Queen Anne's County Planning Commission, the County Commissioners held a public hearing to discuss a proposed ordinance regulating short-term rentals in the county Oct. 22.The intent of the ordinance is to address short-term rentals in the county with a focus on protecting existing neighborhoods and addressing enforcement, according to Stephanie Jones, senior planner.
As of the summer, Queen Anne's County has a total of 181 short-term rentals, she said.
Proposed ordinance regulations include the owner or property manager must be within 25 miles of the property as well as occupancy and guest capacity limits. Guests who are not overnight occupants must vacate by 11 p.m., outdoor amplified music must be discontinued by 8 p.m., and all parking must be on site, Jones said.
Short-term property owners must receive a zoning certificate annually and additional special events approval is separate conditional use, she said.
Short-term rentals must register with the finance office who will collect the hotel tax, Jones said. The proposed ordinance would make short term rental permitted in all county zoning districts and dwelling units and would not supersede any Homeowners Association enforceability.
The planning department is currently working with consultant Granicus and its Host Compliance software to address after hour and weekend response scenarios such as noise, according to Jones. Disturbances will be able to be addressed by calling or filling out an online application for Granicus to contact the property owner directly, she said.
Violations and complaints will be tracked and kept record of, according to Jones.
At public comment, neighbors of Love Point voiced in favor of the proposed ordinance to regulate short term rentals, which they expressed as bringing an increase of traffic hazards and noise complaints to the area.
A key to rental is property management, according to Commissioner Patrick McLaughlin who cited his own experience as a short-term rental owner in Garrett County. In the event of a disturbance, the sheriff's department there has a list of property managers to contact, he said.
In order for a property representative to mitigate a situation as quickly as possible, instead of a 25 mile radius, Commissioner Jack Wilson suggested a qualified agent live in the county, noting the possibility of Bay Bridge traffic backup, "Our citizens shouldn't be inconvenienced by that," he said.
This is the commissioners first stab at a short-term rental ordinance and they can return at a later date to discuss and tweak it as necessary, Commission President Jim Moran said.
"We're not casting a net to stop short-term rentals, we're casting a net to stop those who are abusing the short term rentals to the point where they're disrupting all the homeowners and the citizens of Queen Anne's County," he said.
Moran noted a change in the times, with more property owners coming across the Chesapeake Bay Bridge to buy homes for investments, the quality of life for those already living there should not diminish.
Comments are available to be made before the commissioners vote at the next regular meeting Nov. 12 at 5:30 p.m.

title: Pier Length Changes Could Soon Require Variance
author: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Pier length changes could soon require variance

 March 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 468
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Pier length proved to be a contentious topic during the Queen Anne's County Commissioner's public hearing on a conditional use ordinance on the same.If passed the new ordinance would require approval of a variance for new piers constructed in excess of 150 feet in length.
A variance is a departure from a minimum standard set forth in the Zoning Code and are most often affiliated with a bulk standard like a distance from property lines or the size of an accessory structure, according to Amy Moredock, planning director. Conditional uses are uses listed in each zoning district permitted under certain conditions of the Town Code.
Variances require more unique circumstance standards for the Board of Appeals to review than current conditional use permits, Moredock said.
At the March 12 public hearing, with concerns that longer piers can affect public use of waterways, residents spoke in favor of the ordinance to tighten up reviews for pier extension applications further than the normally allotted 150 feet.
Jay Falstad of the Queen Anne's Conservation Association noted property ownership stops at the shore line and it wasn't unreasonable to ask a landowner to have a higher burden when requesting longer piers.
The change to the ordinance would not automatically deny applications for a longer pier but "puts forth a little bit higher of a standard," he said.
If allowed to go unchecked, longer piers jetting into the water could create an eyesore, and larger boats can utilize marinas, he said.
Billy Benton, vice president of the Queen Anne's County Watermen's Association stated longer piers can impede on the working areas of crabbing and clamming.
On the other side, representing a client that has had a conditional use application in the works for months, Jeff Thompson of Thompson and Richard LLP requested the variance ordinance provide a grandfather condition.
Pier extension requests can be for a number of factors including water depth not just boat size, he said.
His client's request has been in the queue for months and Thompson was worried the variance bill approval would trump that.
It had not been the Board of Appeals' intention to "pull out the rug" from under current conditional use applicants with the proposed amendment, Moredock, said, noting it had not been realized that projects in the pipeline would be affected by the ordinance.
"Since 2002, we've had 45 conditional use applications for pier extensions greater than 150, all were approved. The greatest distance was 495," Long Range Principal Planner Stephanie Jones said.
Commissioner Jack Wilson requested additional information about the average pier length requested more than 150 feet.
Public comment will be open until the commissioners will return to discussion at its next meeting March 26.
In other business, the council approved a map amendment to upgrade the sewer and water services of the Foxx Farm property in Sudlersville to permit services on demand, calling it "long overdue."

title: Queenstown Commissioners Talk Cannabis and Chickens
author: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com

Queenstown Commissioners talk cannabis and chickens

 March 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News

 QUEENSTOWN — With the recreational use of cannabis legalized, and following requirements being set in place by the State, towns are now working to put forth local regulations to address its use.Queenstown is one of such municipalities detailing outlines in their zoning ordinance for prospective retail and businesses regulations to follow.
The Queenstown Planning Commission's original proposal permitted sites or sales processing to be on the south side of Route 301.
Queenstown certainly has regulations in place for medical marijuana but not for recreational use, Town Manager Amy Moore said.
The Planning Commission recently brought forward an amendment that would limit dispensaries to the north side of town, to infill properties only, according to Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan.
Similar to current liquor laws to protect children and compromised individuals, the commission originally proposed a blanket 500-foot setback buffer of dispensaries from areas such as schools, libraries and children centers. The council approved sending the dispensary requirement proposal back to the planning commission to revise and reword the intention.
The council noted through communication with the Town of Centreville and discussion with the Queen Anne's Sheriff's Office, since May 2022, the retail cannabis locations in Centreville have not had any notable crime or problems related to cannabis.
In other business, noting rising food costs, during public comment resident Paris Wells expressed interest in changing the town's ordinance to allow for chickens.
Wells noted the benefit of raising chickens as food in the garage and suggested allowances to the town's current ordinance forbidding feathered fowl.
The town's current ordinance against chickens has been in place for decades, but if a petition with 50 percent of residents' support came forward, the council may consider amendments, Commissioner President Alton Hardee said.
The Queenstown Town Commissioners will next meet March 27 at 6 p.m.

 QUEENSTOWN — The Wheatlands project adjacent to Route 50 is growing closer to fruition as the Queenstown Town Commissioners discussed developer rights and responsibilities for the proposed mixed use residential and commercial community development Feb. 28.A concept plan proposes 79 townhouse lots, 20 cottage court units and 77 single-family home lots for developers Waterman Family Limited Partnership to build Wheatlands on a 148-acre tract of land, directly across from the Queenstown Premium Outlets.
Queenstown Town Manager Amy Moore presented a development rights and responsibilities agreement draft for review including outlines of impact fees and donations to the local fire departments.
The town is currently working with the developer on infrastructure needs and the development's contributions are detailed in the agreement, according to Moore.
As part of the agreement, the developer will also give two one-acre storage land parcels for town use.
Wheatlands has been in the pipeline since 1992, when the Waterman Family Limited Partnership bought the land.
The land was annexed into Queenstown in 2014, which had the backing of the Queen Anne's County Commissioners at the time. But new members won election to the county seat later that year, and they reversed approval of the development.
Waterman and Queenstown fought the reversal but ultimately lost in court, with the Maryland Court of Appeals enforcing a five-year stay on the zoning of the property.
When those five years were up in November 2019, the development proposal moved forward introducing concept plans and architectural guidelines in 2020.
The master concept plan approved by Queenstown in 2021, showed no strong opposition to it from local residents.
Public hearings were held after planning commission members found the master concept plan consistent with the town comprehensive plan.
During those hearings in 2021, Barry Waterman, the proprietor of Waterman Family Limited Partnership, the property owners, told the commissioners, homes will vary in size but will resemble the historic architecture of Queenstown.
More discussion and potential agreement approval is expected at the commissioner's next meeting March 12.

title: Odor Lingers as Centreville Addresses Cannabis Facility
author: Hannah Combs hcombs@chespub.com
content:
Odor lingers as Centreville addresses cannabis facility

 January 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: HANNAH COMBS hcombs@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 735
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — An acrid smell has been lingering in the air over Centreville, and residents affected haven't been afraid to raise a stink. The unpleasant, to some, odor has been the topic of several town council meetings, the latest on Jan. 4.Although there is no ordinance governing odor control — as noted by council member Dan Worth — what was stirring the pot was the proposed ordinance to amend the Town's zoning to only allow indoor agriculture as a permitted use in the Planned Business District.
Ordinance 05-2023, if passed, would potentially restrict Centreville's largest private employer, Green Thumb Industries from expanding their outdoor grow facility in the business park. Council ultimately withdrew the ordinance, following a motion made by member Jeff Kiel and seconded by Eric Johnson.
Green Thumb Industries appeared before council in September of last year to address how those odors could be mitigated.
Speaking on behalf of the cannabis grower, at the Jan. 4 meeting, Jeremy Kacuba, told council they had met with residents of Symphony Village, the largest contingent of residents affected by the odors, last month. A third party firm was recruited by Green Thumb to offer potential solutions to the emanating odors.
Those concerns brought forth by the community are real and have been identified by engineers, Kacuba said, as concentrated processes within the facility. There are some lab processes for the extraction of cannabis oils and further processing, those are the "predominant sources," he said, but the outdoor grow in and of itself is "insignificant" in terms of contribution of odor into the community.
Kacuba noted, there is one concentrated process within the outdoor grow that was identified and is a part of their proposed mitigation solution where plants are brought down during the harvest time and dried to allow for further processing. There is a significant concentration in those drying trailers that can be easily mitigated with the engineering solution Green Thumb Industries has come up with, he said.
The solution recommended by Green Thumb's engineers is not inexpensive, Kacuba said, and would require an initial upfront investment associated with ongoing operational and testing expenses. "(We're) ready to move forward with that solution...a cost we're willing to bear to be a good neighbor to Centreville."
Rebecca Brown, senior management with Green Thumb Industries, told Council they are committed to hearing concerns and being able to address them.
"Filtration systems and molecular atomizers...are not cheap...we've allocated the capital. We've taken this to the strictest regulations in the municipalities we already operate in," Brown said.
Regardless of the council's vote on Ordinance 05-2023, Green Thumb representatives assured the Town they would be moving forward with odor control with a target goal of "elimination."
Kacuba said the company was prepared to "execute the initial capital solution" within approximately two months and then move towards monitoring, with the intent to have odor control systems fully operational in June; noting late summer and fall is when the largest potential of emission related to the outdoor grow process could occur.
There are approximately 200 employees at the Centreville site, established in 2016, responsible for growing, harvesting and processing cannabis. Their operations are run much like an FDA food processing facility would be required, Kabuca said.
Kacuba addressed monitoring and outlined a strategy where samples would be collected based on the recommendation of the engineering specialists. Then lab testing by the third party will track those metrics, and that information will be shared with the town.
During the public comment portion of the meeting, residents again voiced their concerns.
Pat Fox of Symphony Village said she had noticed a lot of strong odor lately and asked if any attempts had been made to mitigate the odor to date.
Another Symphony Village resident, Joe Sikes, said, "not meant to be rude, another source of smell has been the smell of the clothing on the workers."
Mark Emerson of Cloverfields suggested data is how decisions should be made and requested "Council set rigorous standards" for those testing measures.
Addressing Council directly, Symphony Village resident Julie Seymour asked if the town could implement a reporting system similar to the toll-free number used in Delaware for poultry farms.
Council President Ashley Kaiser encouraged those calls to be "politely" reported to Town Hall.
Also addressing Council, Joe Brown, Symphony Village resident, said "We seem very quickly to have gotten this solution" — a solution he was cautious was real.
Kaiser said she thinks complaints drove the solution, but she is hopeful that it will resolve the issue.

 Looking at future wastewater capacity, the Queen Anne's County commissioners on Aug. 12 approved a temporary moratorium on residential and mixed-use development.With the area Wastewater Treatment Plant near capacity, the commissioners adopted a moratorium on applications, approvals, construction, expansion, processing or issuance of subdivision, concept plan, site plan or building permit applications for residential or mixed-use projects in Kent Narrows, Stevensville, Grasonville, Prospect Bay, Cloverfields, Bay City and Southern Kent Island.
During the moratorium, the county will not process, consider, review or approve any application, permit or other approval under the County Zoning Ordinance or the Adequate Public Facilities Ordinance for any project in those subdistricts where the total anticipated sewerage allocation exceeds 1,750 gallons per day.
The resolution does not apply to any pending project that already has prerequisite sewer and water allocation for its specific development.
Queen Anne's County has applied for a rerating of the wastewater treatment plant, which if granted would increase capacity by 300,000 gallons per day.

The county is in the process of updating its 2011 Comprehensive Water and Sewerage Plan. Both that plan and the County Water and Sewerage Allocation Policy may be revised to reflect limited treatment capacity, limited expansion potential and the need to determine how best to allocate sewerage capacity to meet current and future demands.
The county's Adequate Public Facilities Ordinance regulates development based on public infrastructure availability. Commission President Chris Corchiarino said a number of factors have developed since the ordinance was last reviewed, including limited sewer capacity.
With Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the county has also seen an exponential increase in education costs.
"At a time when our enrollment is not going up, our costs have gone up significantly, and that's a cost that is borne by all the citizens," Corchiarino said.
The moratorium will give the county's planning and zoning staff time to take a closer look at zoning, he said.

Funding will be provided entirely by the Rural Legacy grants program through Program Open Space.
The Thompson Farms LLC property is within the Lands End Rural Legacy Area and will add to the 5,085 acres already preserved. The package includes the Agreement of Sale and Project Agreement signed by the commissioners.

Old Love Point Park will see new field lighting. The Department of Parks and Recreation was authorized to contract with Musco Sports Lighting to upgrade the Field Three lights to LEDs for $200,566.

 DENTON — Caroline County wants to hear the public's opinion before making any big decisions on the potential regional detention center agreement with Kent and Queen Anne's counties.The Caroline County Commissioners discussed the draft agreement for the potential facility for the second week in a row at their weekly meeting Tuesday.
County Administrator Kathleen Freeman and County Attorney Stewart Barroll attended a meeting with Queen Anne's County officials about the draft agreement for the detention center Monday, bringing with them a list of concerns from the commissioners.
Freeman was not in attendance for Tuesday's commissioners meeting, but Barrol and Deputy County Administrator Daniel Fox presented an update on what was discussed in the meeting Monday.

To remove one or both of the other counties from the agreement, according to the draft, Queen Anne's County must give the other county a two-year notice to take all their prisoners and house them somewhere else.

title: Shore Residents Share Mixed Views on New Chesapeake Bay Bridge
author: Andrea Grabenstein
content:
Shore residents share mixed views on new Chesapeake Bay Bridge

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1059

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — Informational displays lined the walls of Kent Island High School's cafeteria Wednesday, laying out narrowed-down options for a new Bay Bridge.The self-paced open house welcomed the community to gather information and submit feedback as the Maryland Transportation Authority conducts Tier 2 of the Chesapeake Bay Crossing Study. The study, launched in 2017, seeks to examine the state's options when it comes to the aging bridge.
Melissa Williams, Maryland Transportation Authority director of the division of planning and program development, said the team that developed the various plans for the new bridge went through in-depth analysis on the traffic data gathered throughout the year. It has developed seven proposed alternatives to the current Bay Bridge, with one alternative being a no-build option.
"We are proposing to remove both existing Bay Bridge spans due to the substantial cost of future maintenance and repair the impact to the traveling public associated with those repairs," Williams said.
Bridge spans, full tunnels, bridge tunnels and double decker bridge options were evaluated during the study. Bridge spans were recommended as construction would have fewer environmental impacts and a lower cost compared to other options. Additionally, the bridge spans would allow for greater flexibility in maintaining traffic during maintenance and emergency response situations.
The proposed alternatives include either a new eight-lane or 10-lane bridge consisting of two spans constructed north or south of the existing bridge.
The proposed alternatives consider bus service improvements, part-time shoulder use, interchange consolidation, park and ride facilities, congestion pricing, and pedestrian and bicycle shared use.
The Kent Island open house marks the third total, and second in-person, open house held by the Chesapeake Bay Crossing Tier 2 Study. On the Dec. 11, 129 attended the meeting. An in-person open house was also hosted at Broadneck High School in Annapolis Dec. 9, with 192 in attendance. In-person open houses followed a virtual open house on Dec. 4, in which 435 individuals logged on.
According to Williams, the open houses provided a transparent view of the project to the community.
"It's great to show lines on paper, " she said.
Patty Baker, of Kent Island, remembers the construction of the westbound span of the Bay Bridge. "It was impressive to watch," she said.
Baker attended several of the study's open houses last year and was interested to see how progress and updates have developed. "I couldn't have dreamed what would happen," she said, noting now the once rural area has become more and more part of a freeway and for so long summer beach traffic has detected weekend activities for locals. With the potential for roadway widening, Baker voiced concerns about areas so close to Route 50 including the Stevensville Cemetery, where her own family plots are. She said she appreciated the open house's layout and staff clarification to questions, particularly as to why the new bridges cannot be placed in different corridors.
"They are doing the best they can with what they are working with," she said.
Attending the project's last open house a year ago, Martin Gleason, of Grasonville, was interested in continual aspects of the project and found it to be very informative in regards to the "when, where, and how."
An area resident of 47 years, Brian H. of Kent Island, considered the potential new bridge "long overdue" and found the study thoroughly researched. He was enthusiastic about how the potential lane widening change would improve traffic flow.
Tom Helfenbein, of Kent Island, found the open house informative and offered suggestions of widening certain merging areas and moving chokepoints down to Route 404. "All consideration seems to stop at the (Queenstown) Outlets," he said.
Despite opportunities for public comment, Jennifer Laird, of Chester, claimed she didn't feel like the opinion of locals was being considered and did not approve of any aspect of the project, stating, "It's going to change everything," including bringing in more people from the western shore. Laird claimed the infrastructure was unequipped to handle the traffic and strongly preferred the new bridge be placed elsewhere.
Cheryl Gover, of Queenstown, voiced concerns of bottlenecking, traffic congestion impacts, and was worried how the proposed bridge shared use path would affect jumpers. Gover also recommended finding ways to create alternative routes off the bridge for locals.
Working in Glen Burnie, Jay Diepenbrock, of Centreville, takes a round trip over the Bay Bridge at least twice a week and knows personally how bad traffic can be. Noting it gets worse before it gets better, Diepenbrock was a little disappointed by the the projected timeline, with scheduled construction completion no sooner than about 2035.
"It will probably happen when I'm too old to be driving," he said. Nonetheless, Diepenbrock was optimistic it would be a much needed improvement for future generations.
Heather Lowe, project manager for the Bay Crossing Tier 2 Study, said a multi-use path for bicycles and pedestrians would be separated from travel lanes by a physical barrier across the more than four-mile bridge.
December open houses serve as formal scoping meetings to hear comments on the issues that will be evaluated in an environmental impact statement, according to Andrew Bing, virtual open house facilitator. Included in the areas of environmental considerations are impacts to natural resources, impacts to parks and recreation areas and impacts on historic properties and archaeological sites.
The Environmental Impact Study will focus on socioeconomic resources and land use, and minority and low income population. After time to consider and evaluate public feedback, a draft impact study is anticipated to be published in November 2025, followed by additional public hearings.
A final environmental impact study and record of decisions are anticipated for fall 2026, along with identified selected alternatives.
The Transportation Authority is anticipating finishing the current phase of the Chesapeake Bay Crossing Study in 2026. Five years of design and permitting would follow with construction anticipated for 2032, Bing said.
Anyone unable to attend the open houses still has time to submit comments through the Chesapeake Bay Crossing Study website. Comments received by Jan. 13 will be part of the study's summarization, Williams said, and comments will continue to be received after this date. "We want to hear what you have to say," she said.
Following the data collection, the study is expected to return with additional open houses next year.
Viewing of the virtual open house is available online. More information, as well as feedback submissions and public comments with personal information redacted are available for viewing at baycrossingstudy.com.
Reporter Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado contributed to this story.

title: State Now Plans to Replace the Chesapeake Bay Bridge with Two New Spans
author: Daniel Zawodny The Baltimore Banner
content:
State now plans to replace the Chesapeake Bay Bridge with two new spans

 November 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Daniel Zawodny The Baltimore Banner | Section: Local News 
 
 820
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Chesapeake Bay Bridge may be iconic, but the state now plans to replace its aging twin spans with two entirely new bridges.The Maryland Transportation Authority has been studying how to ease mounting traffic woes on the bridge that carries tens of thousands of vehicles a day between Anne Arundel County and the Eastern Shore and that often becomes a traffic-snarled nightmare, especially on summer weekends.
Officials initially considered adding a new crossing somewhere else in the state or even a ferry service for cars, but quickly narrowed their options down to using the area of the current span.
On Tuesday, officials further focused their plans, announcing that they would consider six options to replace the older spans, all of which would involve expanding bridge capacity to eight or 10 lanes and eventually tearing down the older bridges. Considerations for public transit use on the future bridge exist but are limited, despite the fact that widening roads alone often fails to relieve traffic congestion over time.
The MDTA, which owns and oversees toll facilities in the state, will hold a series of public meetings — two in-person and one virtual — in December to present and solicit feedback on the six proposals. The public also can submit comments online using this survey link.
The two, four-mile continuous steel truss behemoths that comprise the Chesapeake Bay Bridge have been mainstays for commuters and Marylanders vacationing in Ocean City for decades. Knocking the spans down and replacing them would be one of the state's most ambitious infrastructure projects to date, even considering the upcoming replacement of the fallen Francis Scott Key Bridge.
The southern span — the first to open in 1952 — contains two travel lanes. The parallel northern span later joined it in 1973 with three additional lanes. The MDTA uses a system of lane controls to adjust which direction gets an additional lane based on typical travel patterns.
While the state considered a "no-build" alternative that called for just maintaining the old spans, it's unlikely to be pursued. The alternatives study calls the bridge's existing shoulders "substandard" and states that the 186-foot clearance over the channel won't keep pace with future shipping industry demands.
Maryland Transportation Secretary Paul Wiedefeld previously said that the current structures are close to reaching their "useful lifespan."
Officials plan to raise the vertical clearance for cargo ships, which would align with the plan to replace the Key Bridge, also spearheaded by the MDTA. The agency said the future Key Bridge will have at least 230 feet of clearance, a standard set by the Coast Guard. Ships must pass under both bridges to reach the Port of Baltimore.
Four of the proposed alternatives would increase the number of travel lanes across the Bay to eight. The remaining two call for 10 lanes. Each alternative also includes full-size left shoulders on both spans that could be converted into travel lanes during peak hours. All six involve knocking down the current two spans.
The alternatives differ slightly in location (farther north or farther south) and whether to widen the approaches to the bridge on U.S. 50/301 on the eastern and western shores.
The MDTA is currently evaluating the environmental impacts of each alternative and hopes to get the green light on the selected option by November 2026. Then it can pursue contracts for design and construction, with completion likely sometime in the 2030s.
The agency provided a rough cost estimate of $7.3 billion to build eight lanes across two structures and $8.4 billion for 10 lanes. It would cost roughly $3.8 billion over the next 40 years to maintain the current spans if the state were to pursue the "no build" option.
Officials ruled out other designs and structures such as a tunnel, a bridge-tunnel combo or a double-decker bridge. They also ruled out the possibility of a dedicated right-of-way for trains to go over the future spans.
It doesn't mean transit is not being considered by the MDTA, though. The agency will evaluate possible bus service improvements, including a possible 24-hour dedicated bus lane. It also will continue to entertain the possibility of a shared-use path for pedestrians and bikes, though the agency ruled out the possibility of retaining one of the existing spans as a dedicated pedestrian/bike bridge, citing high maintenance costs.
Tolling may change with the future bridge spans, too.
The agency is considering implementing congestion pricing, which would mean changing the cost of crossing the bridge based on the time of day. The idea is often pushed as a way to incentivize travel during off-peak hours, and thus reduce congestion. Critics often chalk it up as a cash-grab during rush hour.
The public is encouraged to share their thoughts at one of the three upcoming open houses:
Virtual: Wednesday, Dec. 4, 6-8 p.m. at baycrossingstudy.com.In-person: Anne Arundel County: Monday, Dec. 9, 6-8 p.m. at Broadneck High School, 1265 Green Holly Drive, Annapolis.In-person: Queen Anne's County: Wednesday, Dec. 11, 6-8 p.m. at Kent Island High School, 900 Love Point Road, Stevensville.

 EASTON — A bicycle and pedestrian advisory committee will soon be up and running in Talbot County after the Talbot County Council unanimously approved an administrative resolution on last week.Council Vice President Pete Lesher made the request for the resolution, which will create a committee intended to gather community input regarding bike and pedestrian safety and accessibility in Talbot County.

He said the committee will be made up of representatives from varying disciplines, including the farming, business, school and police communities.

title: Upgrades Needed to Handle Wastewater in Centreville
author: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Upgrades needed to handle wastewater in Centreville

 April 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News

 Doubling plant size and finding alternate means of discharging waste are some of the topics as proposed Centreville wastewater treatment plant upgrades come closer to fruition.Along with Whitman, Requardt and Associates, the engineering consultant to the town, Jenial Turner, Maryland Department of Public Works program manager presented information on the upgrades needed to the town's Wastewater Treatment Plant to the Centreville Town Council April 4.
The project to expand the liquid and solids treatment capacity of the plant has been in the pipeline for at least three years, Turner said.
The Centreville wastewater treatment plant was last upgraded and expanded in 2003, and the facility is in significant need of an upgrade, according to Turner.
At this time, approximately 80 percent of the plant's current capacity of .542 MGD (million gallons per day), is being utilized, she said.
A new wastewater treatment plant project proposes an increase of .458 MGD for a total capacity of one MGD.
Currently, the wastewater treatment plant discharges to a local water reuse farm through spray irrigation and Corsica River groundwater disposal, Turner said.
For a capacity increase in that size, the town will have to seek options for discharge and disposal of excess waste as the plant's current groundwater disposal methods would not be sufficient enough to support one million gallons, Turner said.
The public works department and engineers are currently in the process of developing the preliminary engineering report and concept design for the new treatment plant and are currently reviewing comments and feedback received from MDE in December 2023.
Public works continually meets with MDE to discuss year-round stream discharge and is leading interest groups regarding effluent disposal and various options going forward, she said.
Noting the concern citizens can have when told the plant is discharging into the river, "We want to make sure that we are armed with information so that we can provide that to the community," Turner said.
The preliminary engineering report is expected to be finalized by June with the design phase to immediately follow for a year of planning. The construction and permitting bidding phase is proposed to start for the end of the year and be concluded by 2026. Final construction for the wastewater treatment plant is expected to be completed by 2029.
"All while still working on trying to figure out where we're going to dispose of the effluent," she said.
Public works is also continually thinking ahead of continual growth of the town and further adjustments and scalability of the plant's design decades down the line.
Wastewater treatment plant upgrades and expansions have been adopted into the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan.
The total project is estimated at $38 million with grant options currently being explored.
Thus far revenue sources include Bay Restoration Funds in the amount of $14.9 million, congressionally directed spending $2.1 million, and $2 million worth of American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funding.
Council President Ashley Kaiser, who has a background in nonprofits and raising state government funding, encouraged fellow council members to continually advocate on the town's behalf for large projects funding.
"It's an exceptionally challenging budget year in a lot of places, here included," she said.
More information about the wastewater treatment plant is expected to be presented to the council around July.

title: Walk This Way: County Presents Draft Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan
author: Andrea Grabenstein

Walk this way: County presents draft Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan
