title: Proposed Landfill Shocks Nearby Landowners
author: Laura Tayman
content:
Proposed Landfill Shocks Nearby Landowners

 October 23, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 844
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE - At last week's meeting of the Queen Anne's County Commissioners, residents from the Shrewsbury Farm neighborhood in Centreville wanted answers regarding the landfill being planned off of Harper Road."I had no idea about this when I bought my house," said Alex Queller whose home is one mile from the proposed Mid-Shore Three landfill site. "This has turned my world upside down."Residents close to the proposed location were notified three weeks ago of a public information meeting being held on Oct. 4 by the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE). The MDE has a process to review submissions and forward them on to the Maryland Department of the Environment for final approval.The landfill, titled the MidShore Level Three, is a result of an agreement between Queen Anne's, Caroline, and Talbot counties in the 1980's to alternate the operation of landfills for a period of 20 years, with Kent County joining the agreement in 1992.The Talbot Mid-Shore Level One and the Caroline MidShore Level Two have already been in operation. Queen Anne's County is set for Level Three beginning in 2031-2050. The county had identified the proposed landsite in 1993, behind the closed Centreville landfill.The Oct. 4 meeting was an information session only. Held by MDE and the landfill owner's engineering consultant GeoSyntec, attendees learned the county had confirmed the project had all necessary zoning and land use approval and that it conformed to the county's 10-year solid waste plan.The total site is 124 acres, with the landfill at 62 acres and the maximum elevation at 240 feet. The landfill will receive household refuse, solid waste from businesses, bulky waste, land clearing debris, and construction waste.The project is just in Phase I of five phases that would span seven years. There will more geological investigation of the site by an accepted engineer, and the findings will go to the MDE, State Department of Natural Resources, the Army Corps of Engineers, and the Maryland Health Department All documentation will be available on the MDE website and at the Centerville Library.County Commissioner Jack Wilson, who attended the Oct. 4 meeting, said he was open to a public meeting. "This is something the commissioners inherited from 1993, just like you," Wilson said. "I'm for being transparent." He told the attendees that Queen Anne's County has also been talking to the Caroline County government about keeping the present landfill for another 12-15 years. "We're going through the steps we have to at this time."County Administrator Todd Mohn said the landfill is included in the present county comprehensive plan and in the 10-year solid waste plan and as such "has been open to public comment each time."Mohn also noted the county knew 30 years ago "our landfills could not be another New York City.""As a region," said Mohn, "we knew that we would need to have something sustainable. We had to join forces. Talbot County went first, Caroline County then took their turn. They obviously have citizens who live near the present landfill that may not want to see it another 12 years."Shrewsbury Farm resident Anna Queller disputed the proposed landfill meets the county's solid waste plan requirement. Reading from the 2015 solid waste plan, she said when addressing the new landfill that "the county's offices of planning and zoning and waste management should conduct a preliminary review of the site."Attendees questioned whether the county had followed its 2020 Comprehensive Plan which dictated that site must be 1500 feet from a residence and 2500 feet from a portable well."There's no way," said Queller. Resident William Kyle was most concerned with the scope of the proposal. "When I went over the Bay Bridge, I measured the height elevation as being 212 feet. This proposal has the height of240 feet. You wouldn't be able to see anything else in the county."After hearing the concerns of residents' comments, MDE presenter Andrew Grenzer said, "Maybe the county needs to look at this again. But I'm not going to say here that their letter of confirmation is wrong."At the commissioners meeting on Oct. 10, Keith Palmer, a geologist who lives close to the location, told commissioners, "If you took a map of Queen Anne's County and chose a location for the landfill, the Centreville spot would be the last choice. It should be a 'do no harm' policy- not where you will impact people, not where you will impact drinking water, not where you will impact traffic. It's the head of the estuary Island Creek which feeds into the Chester River."Shrewsbury Farm resident Brad Dutton assured commissioners his home is well within the 2500 feet line. "As a parent, I try to instill a set of values in my kids. If they make a mistake, they stop, correct it, and make it right. I believe that moving forward at this point is a mistake.""We're not going away," Anna Queller told the commissioners. "The land that the county purchased for the landfill 30 years ago has changed."

title: Serving, Protecting for 250 Years - The Caroline County Sheriff's Office Celebrates Its Sesquicentennial
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Serving, protecting for 250 years - The Caroline County Sheriff's Office celebrates its sesquicentennial

 November 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1A | Section: News 
 
 979
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - To mark the 250th anniversary of the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, a new badge has been struck, containing symbols of its history dating to colonial Maryland.But the badge itself is a symbol of the long line of sheriffs who have held the office since 1773, when Thomas Hughlett of Greensboro was appointed by the British governor after the county was formed from parts of Dorchester and Queen Anne's counties.Bookending the long blue line is Sheriff Donnie Baker, who, like Hughlett, is also a Greensboro native. He's the county's 77th sheriff.Caroline County Deputy Lt. Jacob Andrew is the unofficial historian of the sheriff's office. And because he's the fifth generation of the Andrew family to serve the office during the past century, he's well-qualified for the job."Jake was just teaching me something," Baker said. "I didn't know that the first sheriff was buried up there (in Greensboro)." According to Andrew's research, Hughlett was a plantation owner appointed to a one-year term by the governor to be in charge of weights and scales because he was deemed trustworthy.Ironically, the next year he became captain of the Caroline County Militia Fifth Company, which encompassed Greensboro, Goldsboro and Bridgetown during the American Revolution.Hughlett later became a judge. He is buried in a crypt in a tiny, privately-owned graveyard in a Greensboro subdivision, the site of the Hughlett family farm.During the Civil War, John Wilson Saulsbury served a two-year term from 1861 to 1863 and was required to swear allegiance to the Union.Andrew said Sheriff James Temple, who served from 1923 to 1926 "was actually a pretty cool guy." A veteran of the Spanish-American War, Temple was known as the walking sheriff."He had the first Buick in Caroline County. He always told everybody that," Andrew said. However, "he hated driving it.So, if he had to go serve a warrant on somebody, he'd walk from Denton to Ridgely, lock them up and walk them back." "The original sheriff's office was pretty much a shed on the courthouse green, and it was very easy to break out of," Andrew said. The lynching on the green of Federalsburg blacksmith Marshall Price following accusations of murder in 1895 prompted the government to build a new jail across Gay Street on the Choptank River, where it stands today.In 1921, William Curtis Andrew, Jacob Andrew's great-great grandfather, became sheriff and served a two-year term. His son, William E. Andrew served from 1938 to 1946 and, following a four-year term by Saulsbury Sparks, served again from 1950 to 1961, dying of a heart attack in his office.William's son Louis C. Andrew served from 1961 to 1994, retiring when he was 70. His son, then-Deputy Charles Andrew, served as acting sheriff until Phil Brown was elected sheriff the following year.Back then, the sheriff and his family lived in the center section of what is now the Caroline County jail. Two wings were added to the large brick structure, but Charles Andrew remembers when the original section was home."I got to know a lot of inmates," he said.He recalls the night his "mother had a fit" when a naked woman was brought in by the state police."They had to come in the front door and walk down the hall which separated the living room and dining room directly back to that one-room office" at the back of the house, he said."I would have been seven or eight" years old, Charles Andrew said. "So, she made my father go to the commissioners, and that's when they put stairs on the side of the building to come in the outside door." "Back then, when my father started, he was only making $2,600 a year," he said. "They had to supply their own vehicle. The only thing the county gave them was a radio that went into their own private car." That center section of the current jail is called the Andrew Building today.Until 1994, both the sheriff's office and jail were under the jurisdiction of the sheriff, according to Charles Andrew. When Brown became sheriff, the county Department of Corrections was formed as a separate agency, and Charles Andrew served as the superintendent for 13 years, after serving in the sheriff's office for 20 years.Charles's son Jacob, now the fifth generation to serve in the sheriff's office, serves the county with almost 50 fellow deputies. After serving in the Air Force, Jacob Andrew joined the sheriff's office and has been on the job for 19 years. "I love it. I love my job," he said.The commemorative badge symbolizes not only his family's history of serving county citizens in the sheriff's office, but a long legacy of the office's commitment to public safety stretching back to the nation's founding.At the five points of the badge's star are a Revolutionary War soldier, the Caroline County Circuit Court building, the original courthouse before the renovations, the original sheriff's office on Gay Street, and the current office, completed in 2021 on Double Hills Road."One of the things that former Sheriff Randy Bounds wanted to do was have a wall of sheriff's (pictures)," Baker said."So I told him that Jake is going to fulfill that dream of his." The sheriff's office is seeking memorabilia from the public for a future museum or showcase. If you have any artifacts, photos or clippings you'd like to share, contact Lt. Jacob Andrew at 410-479-4124 or jandrew@carolinemd.org.

title: ICE Outlines Immigration Enforcement as QA Officials Explore 287(g) Agreement
author: Andrea Grabenstein and Hannah Combs
content:
ICE outlines immigration enforcement as QA officials explore 287(g) agreement

 August 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein and Hannah Combs | Section: Local News 
 
 790
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Stevensville — As Queen Anne's County leaders weigh the possibility of entering a formal partnership with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, community members and officials remain divided.U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Agent James Brooks spoke to a full room July 30 during a Queen Anne's County Republican Central Committee informational session, offering a nonpartisan overview of ICE's operations, national enforcement protocols and local implications.
Brooks, the community relations officer for ICE's Washington and Baltimore field offices, outlined the agency's primary focus on enforcing immigration law as enacted by Congress. ICE is tasked with identifying, arresting, detaining and removing individuals unlawfully present in the United States.
Underscoring the complexity of the issue at hand after decades of interpretation and practice by several White House administrations. "Immigration law is the second most complex set of codes next to tax codes," Brooks said.
reviewing options
In separate interviews, Queen Anne's County Commissioner Chris Corchiarino and Sheriff Gary Hofmann said the county's intent is to "fully comply" with federal mandates. They noted that many components of the 287(g) program — through which local jurisdictions partner with ICE on immigration enforcement — are already being fulfilled within the scope of current capabilities.
For example, there is a designated desk for ICE agents at the county sheriff's office, and at least one recent transfer has been made from the county detention center to immigration officials, officials said.
In July, county leadership assembled a task force to study the 287(g) program. The group — composed of Corchiarino, Hofmann, legal counsel and a representative from the detention center — is evaluating the purpose of such an agreement, the potential fiscal impact and any legal liabilities.
Corchiarino said the county commissioners would be required to vote before entering into any agreement. That vote could take place as early as this fall. He added that any needed funding could be drawn from the existing budget.
"As a sheriff, my commitment is to foster a safe environment for all members of our community, regardless of their citizenship status," Hofmann said. "We recognize the complexities of immigration laws and the impact they can have on federal funding. Our priority is to protect our citizens from gangs, criminals and violent offenders while also showing compassion and support for our immigrant community."
Understanding ICE operations
Brooks explained that ICE's operational components include Enforcement and Removal Operations, which conducts arrests and removals, and Homeland Security Investigations, which investigates transnational crimes.
"We don't go out and see who we can arrest," Brooks said. "We already know who we are targeting when ICE is going out to effect arrests."
He stressed that ICE detention is meant to streamline the deportation process, not to punish.
However, due to Maryland's "Dignity Not Detention" law, ICE must seek out-of-state facilities for detainees, oftentimes in Pennsylvania or Virginia.
Maryland has no ICE detention centers, only field holding offices — meaning the Baltimore and Salisbury centers for ICE do not contain beds and are not designed to house detainees past a temporary hold. The goal aims to transfer individuals "within hours," Brooks said. But he could not confirm what current protocol and practices are at those offices.
At press time, ICE had not responded to follow-up inquiries about these procedures.
The removal process, he noted, is far more involved than simply returning an immigrant to their country of origin. It often includes considerations for asylum, travel documentation, legal proceedings before an immigration judge, and agreements with third-party countries.
Brooks said while ICE officers often face criticism, morale remains high within the Baltimore field office. "Officers are busy but good. They know they're making a difference in their communities by going after the worst of the worst," he said.
He added that some officers choose to wear masks when in public as a personal safety measure due to the agency's current public image.
Community perspectives
The presentation was meant to provide factual, nonpartisan information, according to QACRCC President Helen Bennett.
"I think it counter-balances the misinformation that is out there," Bennett said. "And really, knowledge is power and we need to get information that is real, viable and truthful."
Bennett said she was particularly surprised to learn about the lack of ICE detention centers in Maryland, calling out-of-state transfers "a pretty penny." She noted that many attendees expressed interest in learning more about forming a 287(g) agreement.
Committee member Rick Bowers voiced his personal belief that the county should "fully engage" with ICE to enhance public safety and federal resource access.
Conversely, Queen Anne's County Democratic Central Committee Chair Elaine McNeil said her committee opposes entering into a 287(g) agreement.
"They just want a new start. And we're all trying to enjoy that ourselves," McNeil said of immigrants. She expressed concern that individuals could be "unlawfully processed and treated in a manner like some kind of criminal."
The topic remains under discussion by the Democratic committee, she said.
